Question: What is the relationship between gloss and representation error?
Evidence:
[E1] (text, Section 5.2, page 6): Tbl. 1 , top part, shows results as mean error across the data set. We see that for all data sets our method is a better representation in terms of having a lower DSSIM error. The difference in error is more pronounced for N OVEL V IEW than for S AME V IEW . A detailed plot of error distribution is seen in Fig. 6 , left. This is, as classic reﬂectance map captures appearance for a ﬁxed viewer location, for changing geometry, but does not generalize when the viewer moves. Arguably, classic RMs look qualitatively plausible without a reference, but only have low quantitative similarity (SSIM) in novel views.
[E2] (text, Section 1, page 1): The visual appearance of an object depends on the combination of four main factors: viewer, geometry, material and illumination. When capturing and processing appearance, one wishes to change one or more of those factors and predict what the new appearance is. This can be achieved using methods ranging from implicit image-based representations [ 6 , 13 ] to explicit Computer Graphics-like representations [ 27 ]. Implicit methods take a couple of photos as input and allow to predict high-quality imagery in a limited set of conditions, but modest ﬂexibility, e. g., interpolating an image between two photos but not extrapolating to new views. Explicit representations allow for more ﬂexibility when acquiring Phong parameters and HDR illumination maps [ 27 ], but incur substantial acquisition effort, e. g., taking a large number of calibrated (HDR) photos. DAMs propose a new direction to represent appearance:
[E3] (text, Section 6, page 8): We have collected a second dataset of photographs of spherical objects with complex appearance (glossy objects under natural light). In particular we use 3 different materials and 5 different illuminations each with 5 images from registered views (Fig. 11 ) for training and 70 for testing. Please see the supplemental video for the animation. Transfer of appearance captured from a real world image sequence to other complex geometry is shown in Fig. 12 . Tbl. 2 summarizes the outcome for the representation task previously explored for synthetic data only. An example result is seen in Fig. 1 , more are shown in the supplemental materials. claims.text: The relationship between gloss and representation error is shown in Figure 10, where the DSSIM error decreases as the gloss level increases.

cites.observation: The figure shows a relationship between gloss and representation error, with DSSIM error decreasing as the gloss level increases.

claims.text: The representation error is lower for high gloss objects compared to low gloss objects.

cites.observation: The figure shows a decreasing trend in DSSIM error as the gloss level increases, indicating lower representation error for high gloss objects.

claims.text: The representation error for the 'Test' data set is consistently lower than for the 'Total' and 'Train' data sets across all gloss levels.

cites.observation: The figure shows that the 'Test' data set has a lower DSSIM error compared to the 'Total' and 'Train' data sets across all gloss levels.

claims.text: The representation error for the 'Same' view is lower than for the 'Novel' view for all methods and data sets.
